subject: Parking Strategies in Zoning Reform
overview: The board hosted an information session to discuss potential parking and transportation demand management strategies for the city's broader zoning reform project. Consultants presented regional comparisons and gathered community feedback on parking minimums, neighborhood impacts, and environmental considerations, though no formal proposal was voted on.

items.title: Introduction and Session Goals
items.summary: Chair Kit Collins explained the meeting was intended to define terminology and gather community input on parking and transportation strategies before a formal zoning proposal is drafted.

items.title: Presentation on Regional Parking Comparisons
items.summary: Consultants presented data comparing Medford's current off-street parking requirements with neighboring municipalities like Cambridge, Somerville, and Arlington.

items.title: Parking Management Strategies and Definitions
items.summary: The presentation outlined various zoning tools, including maximum parking ratios, compact car space requirements, transit-based reductions, and long-term transportation demand management (TDM) programs.

items.title: Public Comment: Neighborhood Impacts and Car Dependency
items.summary: Residents expressed concerns about the necessity of cars for suburban commuters and the potential for reduced off-street requirements to increase congestion in existing neighborhoods.

items.title: Public Comment: Environmental and Stormwater Concerns
items.summary: Speakers highlighted the environmental impact of impervious surfaces and urged the city to consider stormwater runoff costs when mandating parking minimums.

items.title: Public Comment: Business Accessibility and Public Notification
items.summary: Participants discussed the importance of accessible parking for small businesses and criticized the confusion caused by simultaneous meeting notices from the City Council and the board.

items.title: Public Comment: Housing Density and Eliminating Minimums
items.summary: Advocates for housing density argued that eliminating parking minimums is essential to lower development costs and address the climate emergency.
